summary:
Peru does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity, which has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, applicable to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Anti-discrimination and hate-crime coverage for LGBT people is weak and contested. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity with effect from 7 January 2017, through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code. Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, and although President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in criminal law.

Public facilities are restricted by statute. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, restricting trans people's use of public bathrooms. The resulting Law Nº 32331, enacted 13 May 2025 and known as the Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents, requires restroom entry to be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. A parallel package of bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by Muñante and Montoya, carried the same bathroom and signage prohibitions.

Human Rights Watch reports that vague child-protection articles in the same law, including article 4 on media and advertising and article 5, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and that the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; the organisation assesses child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. The health ministry's own guidance has moved in the opposite direction: in May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare, and after protests the Ministry of Health revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification, removing pathologising terminology from official guidance.

The Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia institute (IDEHPUCP) assesses the bathroom article as open discrimination against trans and non-binary people that implicitly frames them as harassment risks, and cites Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, which holds that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The same analysis records dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Recorded violence is rising. A July 2024 report found that hate crimes increased in Peru with trans women the most affected; its co-author, trans human-rights defender and journalist Gianna Camacho, stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, an occupation associated with elevated exposure to violence.

Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, was raped and tortured by police; in December 2025 three officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. The judgment is Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per reporting, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal gender recognition is partly available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November 2016, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Protection machinery exists alongside official hostility. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck down an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination, and that the April 2025 NGO foreign-funding law allows authorities to revoke registrations on 'public order or security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising. Public hostility is also visible in media: Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo harassed the first openly lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's failure to maintain LGBT anti-discrimination provisions places it with Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American countries lacking such coverage, a comparative position that distinguishes it from most of the subregion.

Public advocacy continues under these constraints. Community demands recorded alongside the 2025 bathroom votes included reliable HIV medication supply, the scrapping of outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office. Pride marches have been held annually since 2002, with a recorded demonstration as early as 1984.

Public opinion shows a generational split: 18–24-year-olds rated 66% favourable toward homosexuals against 49% of the population overall, and approval of same-sex marriage, recorded at 8.3% nationally in 2010, was higher among younger respondents. The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender, describing sexual orientation as the product of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and not a voluntary choice.

Congressional pressure against therapeutic abortion at the Instituto Materno Perinatal continues alongside the gender-related measures, indicating a broader legislative push on sexual and reproductive rights.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is available in part: name change to match gender identity is permitted, and since the Constitutional Court's 21 October 2016 ruling, published 8 November 2016, gender markers on national identity documents may be changed through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. Passports and other identity documents have been the stated subject of a Gender Identity Law introduced 4 November 2016, still pending as of March 2021.

The Ministry of Health reclassified 'transsexualism' as 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance purposes and removed outdated pathologising terminology from official guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients; in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases.

Conversion therapy is prohibited for medical professionals in Peru. Trans Peruvians, and LGBT people generally, live with Law Nº 32331 in force since 13 May 2025, which governs which restroom they may use in public buildings and prohibits signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

NGO registration became contingent on funding rules in April 2025, when authorities gained power to revoke registrations on public-order and security grounds. Economic precarity is documented: 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao were found to work in sex work in a 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two unresolved points in the sources concern the hate-crime provisions. One account holds that Congress's May 2017 vote to strip Articles 46 and 323 failed against President Kuczynski's veto, while another records the LGBT protections as removed from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a one-million-signature removal petition. Which of the two describes the final legal position after the Penal Code's reworking is not settled by the available material.

The numbering of the bathroom bills differs across sources: one cites bills 6506 and 8457, another cites 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR. Whether Law Nº 32331 of 13 May 2025 and the April 2025 'sexual integrity' law described by Human Rights Watch are the same instrument is not confirmed in the inventory.

The status of the Gender Identity Law after March 2021, and whether any of its provisions have since been enacted, is not sourced here. The reported date range for the Azul Rojas Marín attack, described as 'nearly 20 years' before the December 2025 sentence, is taken from press reporting rather than the judgment text.

Hate-crime figures are acknowledged by their own authors as a sub-registry, so the recorded number of incidents against trans women understates actual incidence; no independent national tally is available in the inventory.
